title: Cell division restores the ratio of surface to mass

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Cell division restores the ratio of surface to mass

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Cell division keeps the ratio between a cell's surface and its mass approximately constant and restores the balance of surface energy with the cell's other energies; cleavage of an egg increases surface without increasing volume or mass.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: cell division keeps S/M \approx \text{const}; cleavage increases S at constant V and M

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In short, however it may be brought about, the phenomenon of division of the cell will be precisely what is required to keep approximately constant the ratio between surface and mass, and to restore the balance between the surface-energy and the other energies of the system.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Cell division and surface-mass ratio”. Scope: dividing cells, including cleaving eggs

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: cell division keeps S/M \approx \text{const}; cleavage increases S at constant V and M

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-15: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.59

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The surface-to-volume consequence is straightforward to test with existing 3D images and standard segmentation. The mechanistic claim that division restores an energy balance is much less discriminating and usually lacks the necessary energetic data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Segment cells through growth and division, calculate surface-area-to-volume ratios before and after cytokinesis, and test whether division restores a characteristic ratio without changing total volume. The geometric component is supported by an increased total surface and restored ratio, but the proposed energy-balance cause requires independent energetic measurements.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Segmentation resolution limits true membrane surface estimates.

Geometry alone cannot identify surface-energy balance as the cause of division.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.65
data existence: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Mother-daughter sizes are widely measured, so the geometric effect of cleavage is immediately checkable and will generally hold. That success does not discriminate the claim that division happens in order to restore surface energy, because other division triggers produce the same surface increase. The energetic half remains only partly testable with existing size data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure surface and volume of a cell before and after division, including cleaving eggs. An increase of surface at constant volume confirms the geometric clause. The further claim, that division restores a characteristic surface-to-mass ratio and an energy balance, requires that division be better predicted by departure of that ratio than by genome content or a timer.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Surface and volume do not identify an energetic purpose of division.

A surface increase at cleavage, with mass held constant, is nearly guaranteed by geometry.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.45
data existence: 0.6
operationalizability: 0.65
analysis feasibility: 0.6
